Header.CaseTitle: Thompson v Clearview Credit Services Ltd

Counsel.Lead: Elizabeth Roberts KC; William Taylor (instructed by Allen & Overy LLP)

SummaryOfPosition.Summary: The Appellant seeks compensation under the UK GDPR for distress and damage caused by the Respondent's unlawful processing of her personal data, including inaccurate credit information that caused her to be refused a mortgage.

FactsReliedOn.item: The Respondent is a credit reference agency that held data about the Appellant.
In March 2023, the Appellant discovered that the Respondent had incorrectly recorded a County Court Judgment against her from 2019.
The CCJ related to a different individual with a similar name and had been wrongly attributed to the Appellant.
As a result of this error, the Appellant was refused a mortgage in April 2023.
Despite multiple requests, the Respondent took 6 months to correct the error.

Contentions.item: The Respondent processed inaccurate personal data in breach of Article 5(1)(d) UK GDPR.
The Respondent failed to respond to the subject access request within the statutory timeframe.
The Appellant suffered distress and financial loss as a direct result of the data breach.
The Respondent failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures.

AuthoritiesCited.Authority: Vidal-Hall v Google Inc [2015] EWCA Civ 311

Timeline.Event: Matter giving rise to proceedings first arose
Claimant first became aware of the alleged breach
Claim issued in County Court/High Court
First instance hearing before Deputy High Court Judge
Judgment handed down at first instance

SourceExtracts.Quote: The Clearview Credit Services Ltd failed to discharge its duty of care in the circumstances.
The learned judge erred in concluding that the burden of proof had been satisfied.
The evidence before the court clearly established the breach alleged.
